title: Jira vs Plane
comparison_markdown:
# Jira vs Plane (2026)

## Overview
Jira and Plane are two project management tools that help teams organize and track their work. This comparison is useful for teams considering switching from Jira to Plane, possibly due to cost or data ownership concerns. The core use case for both tools is issue tracking and project management, and someone would switch to take advantage of Plane's self-hosted option or cost savings.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Jira charges per user, while Plane is free and self-hosted.
* Data ownership: Plane allows teams to maintain full control over their data, while Jira stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Jira has a more complex setup process, while Plane is relatively simple to set up.
* Scalability: Jira is designed for large teams and enterprises, while Plane is better suited for small to medium-sized teams.
* Integration with Git: Jira has native integration with Git, while Plane relies on third-party integrations.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Jira | Plane |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.75-$14.50/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $387.50-$725/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,550-$2,900/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Jira:**
* Robust feature set
* Native integration with Git
* Large user community
* Good customer support
* Expensive for large teams
**Plane:**
* Free and self-hosted
* Simple setup process
* Full data ownership
* Limited scalability
* Limited native integrations

## When to Choose Each
Jira is a good choice for large teams or enterprises that need a robust feature set and native integration with Git. It is also a good choice for teams that are already invested in the Atlassian ecosystem. Plane, on the other hand, is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams that want a simple, self-hosted project management tool with full data ownership. It is also a good choice for teams on a budget or with limited IT resources.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Jira data in CSV or JSON format.
2. Set up a new Plane instance and configure the necessary projects and workflows.
3. Use a third-party import tool, such as the Plane Importer, to import your Jira data into Plane.
4. Test and verify that all data has been imported correctly.
5. Update any custom workflows or integrations to work with Plane.

## Our Take
Plane is not yet production-ready for most users, as it lacks some of the features and polish of Jira. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Plane's API is still in development, which may limit its integrations with other tools. However, for small to medium-sized teams with simple project management needs, Plane is a good choice due to its cost savings and self-hosted option.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't need native Git integration
* Teams on a budget that want to save on per-user costs
* Teams that value full data ownership and self-hosting
* Teams with limited IT resources that want a simple setup process
* Teams that don't need advanced features like agile project planning

## FAQ
### Is Plane free?
Yes, Plane is free and self-hosted.
### Can I integrate Plane with Git?
Yes, but only through third-party integrations.
### Is Plane suitable for large teams?
No, Plane is better suited for small to medium-sized teams.
### Can I export my Jira data to Plane?
Yes, you can export your Jira data in CSV or JSON format and import it into Plane.
### Is Plane production-ready?
Not yet, as it lacks some features and polish compared to Jira.
meta_description: Plane, a free self-hosted project management tool, offers cost savings and data ownership. See full comparison or Free migration guide.

title: Trello vs WeKan
comparison_markdown:
# Trello vs WeKan

## Overview

Trello is a visual kanban board tool from Atlassian, simple and beginner-friendly. WeKan is an open-source kanban board offering the same card/list/board model without vendor dependency.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Trello paid plans start at $5/user/month; WeKan is completely free
- **Data control**: WeKan runs on your own server; Trello data lives on Atlassian infrastructure
- **Features**: Trello has a larger Power-Ups marketplace; WeKan covers core kanban features
- **Setup**: Trello requires zero setup; WeKan requires a server
- **Customization**: WeKan open-source code can be extended; Trello cannot

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Trello | WeKan |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $5+/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Trello

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### WeKan

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [wekan/wekan](https://github.com/wekan/wekan) * ~20k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Trello if:** Trello suits individuals and small teams wanting instant zero-setup kanban with integrations to Slack, Google Drive, and GitHub.

**Choose WeKan if:** WeKan is ideal for teams wanting full data ownership or air-gapped deployments.

## Migration Path

Export Trello boards as JSON, then use WeKan Trello importer in Settings to recreate boards, lists, and cards.

## Our Take

WeKan is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Trello tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your WeKan instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Trello, switching to self-hosted WeKan will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Trello until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Trello paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is WeKan free to use?
Yes. WeKan is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Trello to WeKan?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Trello data, follow the WeKan import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does WeKan get regular updates?
Yes. WeKan has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use WeKan without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if WeKan development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced June 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Trello](https://trello.com) and [WeKan](https://wekan.github.io) before making decisions.*
meta_description: WeKan is a free, self-hosted alternative to Trello. Compare pricing, features, and migration steps. See full comparison.

title: Dropbox vs Nextcloud
comparison_markdown:
# Dropbox vs Nextcloud (2026)

## Overview
Dropbox and Nextcloud are two popular cloud storage solutions that enable users to store, access, and share files from anywhere. This comparison is ideal for individuals and teams looking to switch from a proprietary cloud storage service to a self-hosted solution, with the core use case being secure and private file sharing. The key reason someone would switch is to gain full control over their data and reduce costs in the long run.

## Key Differences
* **Cost**: Dropbox charges a monthly fee per user, while Nextcloud is free to use with self-hosting options.
* **Data Ownership**: Nextcloud allows users to retain full ownership and control over their data, whereas Dropbox's terms of service grant the company certain rights to user data.
* **Setup Complexity**: Nextcloud requires more technical expertise to set up and manage, especially for self-hosting, compared to Dropbox's straightforward sign-up process.
* **Scalability**: Nextcloud can be more scalable than Dropbox, especially for large teams and organizations, as it can be hosted on-premises or in a private cloud.
* **Integration with OnlyOffice**: Nextcloud has a native integration with OnlyOffice for document editing, whereas Dropbox relies on third-party integrations like Microsoft Office Online.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Dropbox | Nextcloud |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $9.99-$16.58/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | Approximately $499.50-$829/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | Approximately $1999.60-$3316/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Dropbox:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Wide range of third-party integrations
* Robust security features
* Good customer support
* Limited control over data ownership
**Nextcloud:**
* Self-hosting options for full data control
* High scalability and flexibility
* Native integration with OnlyOffice
* Free to use with self-hosting
* Steeper learning curve due to technical requirements

## When to Choose Each
Dropbox is ideal for small to medium-sized teams that prioritize ease of use and don't require full control over their data. It's also suitable for individuals who need a simple, user-friendly cloud storage solution. On the other hand, Nextcloud is perfect for large teams, enterprises, and organizations that require high scalability, flexibility, and full control over their data. It's also ideal for users who value data privacy and security.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Dropbox data in ZIP format using the Dropbox website or a third-party tool like Dropbox Exporter.
2. Set up your Nextcloud instance, either self-hosted or through a provider.
3. Use the Nextcloud WebDAV interface or a third-party tool like Rclone to import your Dropbox data.
4. Configure any necessary settings, such as user accounts and permissions.
5. Test your Nextcloud instance to ensure all data has been migrated correctly.

## Our Take
Nextcloud is a production-ready solution for most users, offering a wide range of features and high scalability. However, it's essential to be aware of the technical limitations, such as the need for self-hosting and maintenance, which can be a challenge for non-technical users. For users who value data control and security, we recommend switching to Nextcloud, especially for large teams and organizations. However, small teams and individuals who prioritize ease of use may not need to switch.

## Who Should Switch
* Large teams (50+ users) that require high scalability and flexibility
* Enterprises that need full control over their data
* Organizations that prioritize data security and privacy
* Teams that require native integration with OnlyOffice
* Users who want to reduce costs in the long run

## FAQ
### Can I use Nextcloud for free?
Yes, Nextcloud is free to use with self-hosting options. However, you'll need to consider the costs of server maintenance and upkeep.
### Is Nextcloud more secure than Dropbox?
Nextcloud offers robust security features, but the level of security ultimately depends on the user's configuration and self-hosting setup.
### Can I migrate my Dropbox data to Nextcloud automatically?
There are third-party tools available that can help migrate your Dropbox data to Nextcloud, but the process may require some manual configuration.
### Does Nextcloud have a user-friendly interface?
Nextcloud's interface is user-friendly, but it may require some time to get accustomed to, especially for non-technical users.
### Is Nextcloud suitable for small teams?
While Nextcloud can be used by small teams, it may be overkill for teams with simple cloud storage needs, and the self-hosting requirements may be a challenge.
meta_description: Nextcloud, a free self-hosted cloud storage solution, offers more control and security than Dropbox. See full comparison or Free migration guide.

# Airtable vs NocoDB (2026)

## Overview
Airtable and NocoDB are two popular database management tools used for organizing and tracking data. This comparison is beneficial for individuals and teams looking to switch from Airtable to NocoDB, particularly those seeking a self-hosted solution with more control over their data. The core use case for both tools is to provide a flexible and customizable database for various applications, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Airtable offers a free plan and paid plans starting at $10-$20 per user per month, while NocoDB is free and self-hosted.
* Data ownership: NocoDB allows users to have full control over their data, while Airtable stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Airtable has a more user-friendly interface and is easier to set up, while NocoDB requires more technical expertise.
* Scalability: NocoDB is highly scalable and can handle large amounts of data, while Airtable has limitations on its free plan.
* Feature difference: NocoDB has a built-in GraphQL API, while Airtable has a REST API.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Airtable | NocoDB |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $10-$20/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $500-$1000/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $2000-$4000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Airtable
* Easy to use and set up
* User-friendly interface
* Integrates with many third-party apps
* Limited control over data
* Costs can add up for large teams
### NocoDB
* Self-hosted and free
* Highly scalable
* Built-in GraphQL API
* Steeper learning curve
* Limited support for certain features

## When to Choose Each
Airtable is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams who need a user-friendly database management tool and are willing to pay for it. It's also a good option for those who don't require a high level of control over their data. NocoDB, on the other hand, is suitable for larger teams or organizations that require a self-hosted solution with more control over their data. It's also a good option for those who need a highly scalable database management tool.

## Migration Path
1. Export data from Airtable in CSV or JSON format.
2. Set up a NocoDB instance on your server.
3. Use the NocoDB import tool to import your data from the CSV or JSON file.
4. Configure your NocoDB instance to match your Airtable setup.
5. Test your NocoDB instance to ensure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
NocoDB is not yet production-ready for most users, as it still lacks some features and has a steeper learning curve. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that NocoDB requires a high level of technical expertise to set up and configure. However, for teams who require a self-hosted solution with more control over their data, NocoDB is a good option. We recommend switching to NocoDB if you have a large team and require a highly scalable database management tool, but not if you're a small team who needs a user-friendly interface.

## Who Should Switch
* Large teams (100+ users) who require a self-hosted solution
* Teams who need a highly scalable database management tool
* Organizations who require a high level of control over their data
* Developers who need a built-in GraphQL API
* Teams who don't need a user-friendly interface

## FAQ
### Can I use NocoDB for free?
Yes, NocoDB is free and self-hosted. You can download and install it on your own server.
### Is NocoDB easy to use?
No, NocoDB has a steeper learning curve and requires more technical expertise to set up and configure.
### Can I migrate my data from Airtable to NocoDB?
Yes, you can export your data from Airtable in CSV or JSON format and import it into NocoDB using the import tool.
### Does NocoDB have a user-friendly interface?
No, NocoDB's interface is more technical and requires a higher level of expertise to use.
### Is NocoDB production-ready?
Not yet, NocoDB is still in development and lacks some features.
